cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Latin has six cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, and ablative. Each case signals a different grammatical function.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Nominative: subject of the verb and complement after verbs like sum (e.g. puella currit — the girl runs; puella est Regina — the girl is queen).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Vocative: used for direct address (e.g. O puella! — O girl!). It is usually identical to the nominative except in second declension masculine singular (e.g. Marce, not Marcus).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Accusative: direct object of a transitive verb, and object of many prepositions (e.g. puellam video — I see the girl; ad villam — to the villa).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Genitive: possession or relationship, answering 'of whom?' or 'whose?' (e.g. villa patris — the house of the father / the father's house). Partitive genitive with nouns of quantity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Dative: indirect object, answering 'to/for whom?' (e.g. puellae librum dedi — I gave a book to the girl). Also used with compound verbs and certain adjectives.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Ablative: separation, means, accompaniment, time when/within which, and object of many prepositions (e.g. gladio pugnavit — he fought with a sword; ab urbe — from the city).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Prepositions take either the accusative (motion towards: ad, to; in, into; per, through) or the ablative (position: in, in/on; ex, from; cum, with; de, about/from).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: Some prepositions can take both cases with different meanings: in + ablative = in/on (position), in + accusative = into/onto (motion towards).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Cases & Their Uses
cards.back: The ablative absolute uses a noun and participle in the ablative case to set the background circumstances: urbe capta, milites fugerunt (the city having been captured, the soldiers fled).

cards.front: What should you know about gcse latin exam tips — cases & their uses?
cards.back: 1. For Cases & Their Uses, use a range of vocabulary and complex grammatical structures to access higher marks 2. Check verb tenses, agreements and word order carefully in your written work 3. In translation tasks, translate meaning rather than word-for-word 4. When writing about Cases & Their Uses, include opinions and justifications, not just descriptions 5. For listening and reading, focus on key words and cognates to extract meaning
